landform.simple: A natural feature of the Earth's surface, such as a mountain, valley, or plain.
landform.detailed: A distinct physical shape on the land, formed by processes such as erosion, weathering, or tectonic movement, and used in geography to describe terrain.
landform.example: Uluru is a famous Australian landform that students often study in Year 6 geography.
landform.basic: Uluru is a well-known shape on the land.

rainfall.simple: The amount of rain that falls in a place over a certain time.
rainfall.detailed: A measured quantity of rain, usually recorded in millimetres, that helps scientists and farmers understand climate, drought, and water supply.
rainfall.example: The graph showed that summer rainfall was much lower than usual in the wheat belt.
rainfall.basic: The graph showed that less rain fell in summer.

runoff.simple: Water that flows over the ground instead of soaking in, often after heavy rain.
runoff.detailed: Rainwater or melted water that travels across the land into creeks, drains, or rivers, carrying soil, nutrients, or pollution with it.
runoff.example: After the storm, runoff from the oval carried mud into the school drain.
runoff.basic: After the storm, water ran off the oval into the drain.

bushfire.simple: A dangerous fire that spreads through bushland, grass, or forest.
bushfire.detailed: An uncontrolled fire in vegetation, common in hot, dry Australian conditions, that can threaten habitats, towns, and air quality.
bushfire.example: The class studied how a bushfire can start from lightning on a dry summer day.
bushfire.basic: The class studied how a fire can start in the bush.

cyclone.simple: A powerful spinning storm with very strong winds and heavy rain, often near the coast.
cyclone.detailed: A tropical low-pressure weather system that brings destructive winds, flooding rain, and storm surge; in Australia it is tracked closely in the north.
cyclone.example: A tropical cyclone can close schools across northern Queensland for several days.
cyclone.basic: A huge storm can close schools in the north.

drought-resistant.simple: Able to survive and keep growing when there is very little rain.
drought-resistant.detailed: Describes plants, crops, or designs that cope with long dry periods by storing water, reducing water loss, or growing in harsh soil.
drought-resistant.example: The garden club chose a drought-resistant native shrub that needs little watering.
drought-resistant.basic: They chose a plant that can live with little rain.

native.simple: Originally living or growing in a place, not brought from somewhere else.
native.detailed: Describes plants, animals, or people that belong naturally to a region; in science it often contrasts with species introduced by humans.
native.example: The science group planted native wattles because they suit the local soil and climate.
native.basic: The group planted trees that already belong in this area.

introduced.simple: Brought into a place by people, rather than living there naturally.
introduced.detailed: Describes a species, plant, or practice that humans have moved into a new region, sometimes causing harm to local ecosystems.
introduced.example: Rabbits are an introduced species that damaged Australian farmland and native plants.
introduced.basic: Rabbits were brought here and then caused problems.

endangered.simple: At serious risk of dying out if nothing is done to protect it.
endangered.detailed: Describes a species whose numbers have fallen so low that extinction is a real threat without conservation, habitat protection, or careful laws.
endangered.example: The bilby is an endangered Australian mammal that needs protected habitat to survive.
endangered.basic: The bilby is an animal that might disappear if we do not help.

invasive.simple: Spreading quickly in a new place and harming the plants or animals already there.
invasive.detailed: Describes a non-native species that grows or breeds so successfully that it crowds out local species, damages habitats, or costs communities time and money.
invasive.example: Lantana is an invasive weed that smothers native bush along many Australian creeks.
invasive.basic: That weed spreads fast and crowds out other plants.

sustainable.simple: Able to continue for a long time without using up resources or harming the environment.
sustainable.detailed: Describes a way of living, farming, or making energy that meets present needs while protecting ecosystems so future generations can still use them.
sustainable.example: Using rainwater tanks is a sustainable way for the school to water the garden.
sustainable.basic: Using rainwater is a way to look after water for the future.

biodegradable.simple: Able to break down naturally so it does not stay as rubbish for years.
biodegradable.detailed: Describes a material that microorganisms can decompose into simpler substances, reducing lasting waste compared with plastics that persist in soil and water.
biodegradable.example: The canteen switched to biodegradable plates so picnic rubbish would break down more quickly.
biodegradable.basic: The canteen chose plates that rot away instead of lasting forever.

non-renewable.simple: Unable to be replaced once it has been used up, such as coal or oil.
non-renewable.detailed: Describes a resource that forms so slowly that humans cannot replace it within a lifetime, so using it reduces what future people will have.
non-renewable.example: Coal is a non-renewable fuel, so burning it faster than it forms cannot last forever.
non-renewable.basic: Coal cannot be made again quickly once we burn it.

fair-minded.simple: Willing to listen to both sides and judge people or ideas without unfair favour.
fair-minded.detailed: Describes a person who weighs evidence and other viewpoints calmly, rather than rushing to a biased or one-sided conclusion.
fair-minded.example: A fair-minded marker reads both arguments before deciding which case is stronger.
fair-minded.basic: A good marker listens to both sides before deciding.

even-handed.simple: Treating each side of an argument or dispute with the same care and fairness.
even-handed.detailed: Describes a balanced approach that does not favour one person, group, or claim, especially when evidence or consequences must be compared.
even-handed.example: The chairperson stayed even-handed so both debate teams received equal speaking time.
even-handed.basic: The chairperson treated both teams the same way.

open-minded.simple: Ready to consider new ideas or evidence instead of sticking to one view.
open-minded.detailed: Describes a thinker who can revise a judgement when stronger reasons appear, which is essential in inquiry, debate, and scholarship reading.
open-minded.example: An open-minded scientist changes a hypothesis when the results do not match the prediction.
open-minded.basic: A good scientist can change their idea when the results are different.

well-supported.simple: Backed by clear reasons, facts, or evidence rather than guesswork.
well-supported.detailed: Describes a claim, answer, or argument that is strengthened by relevant proof, examples, or sources, so a reader can see why it is reliable.
well-supported.example: A well-supported conclusion in a science report quotes the measurements, not just an opinion.
well-supported.basic: A strong conclusion uses the measurements, not only what you think.

ill-informed.simple: Based on little knowledge, weak facts, or incomplete information.
ill-informed.detailed: Describes a view, comment, or decision made without enough accurate information, so it is likely to be unfair, mistaken, or easy to challenge.
ill-informed.zh: 消息不灵的；了解不足的
ill-informed.example: An ill-informed opinion about recycling can spread if nobody checks the actual data.
ill-informed.basic: A guess about recycling can spread if nobody checks the facts.

one-sided.simple: Showing only one point of view and leaving out the other side.
one-sided.detailed: Describes an argument, report, or story that presents a single perspective as if it were the whole truth, which weakens fairness and persuasion.
one-sided.example: A one-sided letter about the new bike path ignored residents who needed more parking.
one-sided.basic: The letter only told one side of the bike-path story.

two-sided.simple: Looking at both sides of an issue instead of only one opinion.
two-sided.detailed: Describes a discussion or piece of writing that presents advantages and disadvantages, or competing views, before reaching a reasoned judgement.
two-sided.zh: 正反两面的；兼顾双方的
two-sided.example: The teacher asked for a two-sided discussion of homework so benefits and drawbacks were both heard.
two-sided.basic: The teacher asked us to talk about both good and bad points.

long-lasting.simple: Continuing for a long time without wearing out or disappearing quickly.
long-lasting.detailed: Describes an effect, material, or memory that remains useful or noticeable over an extended period, rather than fading after a short burst.
long-lasting.example: Plastic litter has a long-lasting impact on beaches because it breaks down so slowly.
long-lasting.basic: Plastic rubbish stays on beaches for a very long time.

fast-paced.simple: Moving or changing quickly, with little time to slow down.
fast-paced.detailed: Describes a story, game, or lifestyle whose events happen in rapid succession, creating excitement but sometimes leaving little space for reflection.
fast-paced.example: The opening chapter was so fast-paced that readers barely had time to breathe.
fast-paced.basic: The opening chapter moved so quickly that readers had no time to rest.

slow-moving.simple: Happening or travelling at a gentle, unhurried speed.
slow-moving.detailed: Describes a plot, process, or object that advances gradually; in literature it can build tension, while in science it can describe glaciers, traffic, or change.
slow-moving.example: The slow-moving river deposited rich soil along the floodplain after each wet season.
slow-moving.basic: The river moved slowly and left rich soil on the banks.

closely.simple: With careful attention to small details, or in a near and connected way.
closely.detailed: Used when someone watches, reads, or studies something with precision, or when two ideas, people, or results are tightly linked.
closely.example: Oliver looked closely at the graph before deciding which variable had changed.
closely.basic: Oliver looked hard at the graph before deciding.

carefully.simple: In a thoughtful way that tries to avoid mistakes or harm.
carefully.detailed: Describes an action done with caution, accuracy, and attention, whether measuring in science, choosing words in an essay, or handling evidence.
carefully.example: Measure the liquid carefully so the experiment can be repeated by another group.
carefully.basic: Measure the liquid with care so the test can be done again.

correctly.simple: In the right way, without error or misunderstanding.
correctly.detailed: Describes an action, answer, or procedure that matches the required rule, method, or fact, which matters in tests, science, and formal writing.
correctly.example: Label the axes correctly or the line graph will be hard to interpret.
correctly.basic: Put the right labels on the axes or the graph will be confusing.

equally.simple: To the same degree, or in a way that treats each part or person the same.
equally.detailed: Used when amounts, importance, or treatment are shared without favouring one side; it also links two ideas that deserve the same weight.
equally.example: Both teams were equally responsible for keeping the sports equipment tidy.
equally.basic: Both teams had the same job of putting the equipment away.

firmly.simple: In a strong, steady way that shows you will not easily give in.
firmly.detailed: Describes speech or action that is decisive and stable, used in argument when a writer holds a position clearly without sounding rude or shaky.
firmly.example: In the debate she stated firmly that plastic bags should be banned at the canteen.
firmly.basic: In the debate she said clearly that plastic bags should be banned.

freely.simple: Without being blocked, forced, or tightly controlled.
freely.detailed: Describes movement, speech, or choice that is not restricted by rules, fear, or physical barriers; in HASS it often relates to rights and open discussion.
freely.example: Citizens in a democracy should be able to speak freely about unfair laws.
freely.basic: People in a democracy should be able to talk about unfair laws.

highly.simple: To a great degree; very much, especially when praising or ranking something.
highly.detailed: An intensifier used in academic writing to strengthen an adjective or adverb, as in a very effective method or an unusually striking result.
highly.example: The scholarship paper is highly challenging, so careful planning of each paragraph helps.
highly.basic: The scholarship paper is very hard, so planning each paragraph helps.

honestly.simple: In a truthful way, without hiding facts or pretending.
honestly.detailed: Describes speech or behaviour that matches what a person really thinks or knows; in narrative it can reveal character, and in argument it builds trust.
honestly.example: The narrator honestly admits she was frightened when the river rose overnight.
honestly.basic: The narrator tells us she was frightened when the river rose.

largely.simple: For the most part; mainly, though not completely.
largely.detailed: Used to show that something is true in the main, while leaving room for smaller exceptions, which is useful when explaining causes or patterns.
largely.example: The crop failure was largely due to the long drought, not to poor seed quality.
largely.basic: The crop failed mainly because of the long dry spell.

officially.simple: In a formal, public, or government-approved way.
officially.detailed: Describes an action or statement made with recognised authority, such as a parliament, school, or court, rather than as a private or unofficial comment.
officially.example: Australia officially became a federation on 1 January 1901.
officially.basic: Australia became one nation on 1 January 1901.

partly.simple: To some extent, but not completely or in every way.
partly.detailed: Used when a cause, answer, or description is only a portion of the whole truth, which helps writers avoid overstating a claim.
partly.example: The flood was partly caused by blocked drains as well as the heavy rainfall.
partly.basic: The flood was caused in some ways by blocked drains.

rapidly.simple: Very quickly; happening at a high speed in a short time.
rapidly.detailed: Describes a change or movement that happens in a short time, often used in science for growth, cooling, erosion, or the spread of a process.
rapidly.example: Ice melts rapidly when it is placed in warm water during the heat investigation.
rapidly.basic: Ice melts quickly when it is put in warm water.

safely.simple: In a way that avoids danger, injury, or damage.
safely.detailed: Describes an action carried out with proper care, equipment, or rules so people, animals, or materials are protected from harm.
safely.example: Wear goggles so the class can heat the beaker safely during the inquiry.
safely.basic: Wear goggles so nobody gets hurt when the beaker is heated.

steadily.simple: At a regular, even pace, without sudden stops or jumps.
steadily.detailed: Describes a process that continues in a controlled, consistent way, such as a temperature rise, a heartbeat, or progress on a long task.
steadily.example: The temperature rose steadily as the lamp stayed on the ice for ten minutes.
steadily.basic: The temperature went up evenly while the lamp stayed on.

strongly.simple: With force, confidence, or a high degree of feeling or evidence.
strongly.detailed: Used in argument and science to show that a claim, reaction, or preference is powerful, well-backed, or intense rather than mild.
strongly.example: The team argued strongly that the school should ban single-use plastic bottles.
strongly.basic: The team said with real force that plastic bottles should be banned.

successfully.simple: In a way that achieves the result you wanted.
successfully.detailed: Describes an action that meets its goal, whether completing an experiment, persuading an audience, or solving a problem without major failure.
successfully.example: The group successfully grew seedlings in the drier soil after changing the watering plan.
successfully.basic: The group managed to grow seedlings after changing the watering plan.

widely.simple: By many people or in many places; over a large area.
widely.detailed: Used when an idea, habit, or object is common across a broad group or region, or when something is spread out rather than limited to one spot.
widely.example: Solar panels are now widely used on Australian school roofs to cut electricity costs.
widely.basic: Many Australian schools now use solar panels on the roof.

acknowledge.simple: To admit that something is true, or to show that you have noticed it.
acknowledge.detailed: To accept a fact, source, feeling, or contribution openly, which is important when citing evidence, thanking helpers, or treating other views fairly.
acknowledge.example: Good researchers acknowledge the source of every quotation in the bibliography.
acknowledge.basic: Good researchers say where each quotation came from.

advocate.simple: To speak or write in favour of an idea, person, or change.
advocate.detailed: To support a cause publicly with reasons, asking others to accept a policy, right, or action; the same word can also name a person who does this.
advocate.example: The student council will advocate a later start time with evidence from sleep research.
advocate.basic: The student council will speak up for a later start time.

anticipate.simple: To expect something and get ready for it before it happens.
anticipate.detailed: To think ahead about a likely event, problem, or question so you can plan, warn others, or adjust a method in time.
anticipate.example: Good experimenters anticipate measurement error and write a way to reduce it.
anticipate.basic: Good experimenters think ahead about mistakes and plan how to reduce them.

articulate.simple: To express an idea clearly in speech or writing so others can follow it.
articulate.detailed: To put thoughts into precise words, which is a key scholarship skill when explaining a claim, a feeling, or a complex process.
articulate.example: In the oral, she could articulate why the character's choice felt unfair.
articulate.basic: In the oral, she could explain clearly why the choice felt unfair.

ascertain.simple: To find something out for certain after checking carefully.
ascertain.detailed: To establish a fact through investigation, measurement, or reliable sources rather than guessing, which is central to inquiry and research.
ascertain.example: The class had to ascertain whether the tap water or the tank water was more acidic.
ascertain.basic: The class had to find out for sure which water was more acidic.

assert.simple: To state something firmly as if it is true, especially in an argument.
assert.detailed: To put forward a claim with confidence; a strong writer then supports that statement with evidence rather than leaving it as a bare opinion.
assert.example: Do not merely assert that the law is unfair; give two pieces of evidence.
assert.basic: Do not just say the law is unfair; give two pieces of evidence.

attain.simple: To reach a goal, standard, or level after effort.
attain.detailed: To achieve something that required work, skill, or persistence, such as a score, a qualification, or a scientific result.
attain.example: Regular practice helped him attain a higher score on the scholarship reading paper.
attain.basic: Regular practice helped him reach a higher score.

attribute.simple: To say that a result or quality comes from a particular cause or person.
attribute.detailed: To assign responsibility, credit, or origin to something, as when scientists link a change to a variable or writers credit a quote to its author.
attribute.example: The students attribute the faster growth to extra sunlight, not to a new fertiliser.
attribute.basic: The students say the faster growth came from extra sunlight.

complement.simple: To go well with something else and make it more complete or effective.
complement.detailed: To add a quality or part that fills a gap or improves a whole, which is different from complimenting someone with praise.
complement.example: Clear diagrams complement a written explanation in a science report.
complement.basic: Clear diagrams make a written explanation stronger.

comprise.simple: To be made up of particular parts, or to include those parts.
comprise.detailed: To consist of listed elements that together form the whole, a precise verb for describing groups, texts, or systems without adding extra wording.
comprise.example: The inquiry team will comprise a note-taker, a timer, and two researchers.
comprise.basic: The inquiry team will be made up of a note-taker, a timer, and two researchers.

conceive.simple: To form an idea, plan, or picture in your mind.
conceive.detailed: To invent or imagine something that did not exist yet, from a story plot to a scientific model or a civic proposal.
conceive.example: The class had to conceive a fair way to share the oval at lunchtime.
conceive.basic: The class had to think up a fair way to share the oval.

condemn.simple: To say strongly that something is wrong and should be rejected.
condemn.detailed: To judge an action, idea, or person as morally or legally unacceptable, often in public argument, news, or historical writing.
condemn.example: Many citizens condemn littering in national parks because it harms wildlife.
condemn.basic: Many people say littering in national parks is wrong.

confine.simple: To keep something or someone within limits and not let it spread.
confine.detailed: To restrict movement, discussion, or activity to a set place, time, or topic, whether in a prison, a habitat, or a tightly focused paragraph.
confine.example: Please confine your speech to the water-saving topic so the debate stays fair.
confine.basic: Please keep your speech on the water-saving topic.

consent.simple: To agree to something, especially after you understand what it involves.
consent.detailed: To give permission freely, which in HASS and civic life matters for laws, medical choices, and respectful treatment of other people's rights.
consent.example: Researchers must consent to follow the safety rules before using the lab chemicals.
consent.basic: Researchers must agree to the safety rules before using the chemicals.

contemplate.simple: To think about something quietly and carefully for a while.
contemplate.detailed: To consider an idea, feeling, or choice in a deep, unhurried way, often used in literary description of a character's inner thoughts.
contemplate.example: At dusk the narrator sat on the jetty to contemplate whether she should tell the truth.
contemplate.basic: At dusk the narrator sat on the jetty and thought about telling the truth.

contradict.simple: To say the opposite of another statement, or to clash with the facts.
contradict.detailed: To deny or oppose a claim by offering a conflicting statement or evidence; contradictions weaken an argument unless they are resolved.
contradict.example: Do not contradict your earlier sentence unless you explain why the new evidence is stronger.
contradict.basic: Do not say the opposite of your earlier sentence without explaining why.

cultivate.simple: To grow plants carefully, or to develop a skill, habit, or friendship.
cultivate.detailed: To tend something so it improves over time, from crops in a field to curiosity, kindness, or civic habits in a community.
cultivate.example: Good HASS teachers cultivate curiosity about how everyday laws were made.
cultivate.basic: Good HASS teachers help curiosity grow about how laws were made.

dedicate.simple: To give your time, energy, or a work of art to a special purpose or person.
dedicate.detailed: To commit effort or honour something by setting it aside for a cause, a person, or a goal, often with a sense of loyalty.
dedicate.example: She chose to dedicate her lunch breaks to finishing the scholarship writing task.
dedicate.basic: She used her lunch breaks to finish the writing task.

deviate.simple: To move away from the usual path, plan, or expected result.
deviate.detailed: To differ from a standard, rule, or predicted pattern, which in science can signal error, a new variable, or an interesting anomaly.
deviate.example: If the temperature readings deviate too far from the class average, check the thermometer.
deviate.basic: If the temperature readings are far from the class average, check the thermometer.

devote.simple: To give most of your attention, time, or care to one person or purpose.
devote.detailed: To apply yourself wholeheartedly to a task, relationship, or cause, a stronger, more personal commitment than simply spending time.
devote.example: The coach asked players to devote ten minutes each night to practising free throws.
devote.basic: The coach asked players to give ten minutes each night to free throws.

differentiate.simple: To show or tell the difference between two or more things.
differentiate.detailed: To distinguish items by their features so they are not treated as the same, a precise academic skill in science, grammar, and argument.
differentiate.example: Can you differentiate a fact from an opinion in this news paragraph?
differentiate.basic: Can you tell a fact from an opinion in this news paragraph?

disclose.simple: To make hidden information known, often because it should be shared.
disclose.detailed: To reveal facts that were private, secret, or not yet public, which in civic life can involve honesty, safety, or legal duty.
disclose.example: Witnesses must disclose what they saw if the council is investigating the accident.
disclose.basic: Witnesses must tell what they saw if the council is investigating.

displace.simple: To force something or someone out of its usual place.
displace.detailed: To push people, animals, or objects from the position they occupied, as when a flood displaces families or a new species displaces a native one.
displace.example: Rising floodwater can displace families from low-lying streets within hours.
displace.basic: Rising floodwater can force families out of low-lying streets.

disrupt.simple: To interrupt a process so it cannot continue in a smooth, normal way.
disrupt.detailed: To break the regular order of a system, lesson, habitat, or plan, often causing delay, confusion, or unexpected change.
disrupt.example: A sudden power cut can disrupt the data logger in the middle of an experiment.
disrupt.basic: A sudden power cut can stop the data logger in the middle of a test.

dominate.simple: To have the strongest control, influence, or share in a situation.
dominate.detailed: To be the most powerful or most noticeable part of a group, landscape, market, or debate, sometimes fairly and sometimes unfairly.
dominate.example: A few large companies can dominate the news if smaller voices are not heard.
dominate.basic: A few large companies can take over the news if smaller voices are not heard.

embody.simple: To show an idea or quality clearly through a person, object, or action.
embody.detailed: To give a visible or living form to an abstract value, such as courage or fairness, so readers can see the idea in concrete detail.
embody.example: The quiet hero seemed to embody loyalty when she stayed with her injured friend.
embody.basic: The quiet hero showed loyalty when she stayed with her injured friend.

empower.simple: To give someone the confidence, skill, or right to take action.
empower.detailed: To increase a person's or group's ability to make choices and influence events, often by sharing knowledge, resources, or legal authority.
empower.example: Teaching first aid can empower students to help safely before adults arrive.
empower.basic: Teaching first aid can help students act safely before adults arrive.

enact.simple: To make a proposal into an official law or rule.
enact.detailed: To pass and put into force legislation or a formal policy, a key civic process in parliaments, councils, and school governance.
enact.example: Parliament can enact a law only after both houses have agreed to the bill.
enact.basic: Parliament can make a law only after both houses have agreed.

encompass.simple: To include a wide range of things within one idea, area, or group.
encompass.detailed: To cover or contain several parts so they sit inside a larger whole, useful when defining a topic, a region, or a set of skills.
encompass.example: The inquiry will encompass water use at home, at school, and on local farms.
encompass.basic: The inquiry will include water use at home, at school, and on farms.

endorse.simple: To give public support or official approval to a person, idea, or product.
endorse.detailed: To back something so others see that you judge it acceptable or worthwhile, from signing a petition to a principal approving a plan.
endorse.example: The principal will endorse the recycling plan if the data show it reduces waste.
endorse.basic: The principal will support the recycling plan if the data look strong.

enforce.simple: To make sure a rule or law is actually followed.
enforce.detailed: To apply authority so that people comply with a requirement, using reminders, penalties, or official action when needed.
enforce.example: Rangers enforce fishing limits so fish populations can recover each season.
enforce.basic: Rangers make people follow fishing limits so fish can recover.

enhance.simple: To improve the quality, strength, or value of something.
enhance.detailed: To make a feature better or more effective without replacing it entirely, such as enhancing a paragraph with sharper evidence.
enhance.example: Clear topic sentences enhance a report because each paragraph then has a job.
enhance.basic: Clear topic sentences make a report stronger.

enrich.simple: To make something richer, more interesting, or more valuable.
enrich.detailed: To add depth, nutrients, knowledge, or experience so a soil, a story, or a person's understanding becomes fuller than before.
enrich.example: Vivid sensory details enrich a camp narrative and help the reader feel the cold.
enrich.basic: Vivid details make a camp story more interesting.

entitle.simple: To give someone a right to have or do something.
entitle.detailed: To grant a legal or official claim, such as being entitled to a vote, a refund, or a fair hearing; also used when giving a text a title.
entitle.example: The new law will entitle every citizen aged 18 and over to vote in federal elections.
entitle.basic: The new law will give every citizen aged 18 and over the right to vote.

envisage.simple: To picture a future situation and think about how it could happen.
envisage.detailed: To form a clear mental image of a plan, outcome, or possibility before it exists, a useful verb for design, policy, and academic planning.
envisage.example: Can you envisage a playground that uses less water but still feels fun in summer?
envisage.basic: Can you picture a playground that uses less water but still feels fun?

evoke.simple: To bring a feeling, memory, or image strongly into someone's mind.
evoke.detailed: To call forth an emotional or sensory response through words, music, or images, a key literary technique in narrative and poetry.
evoke.example: The smell of wet eucalyptus can evoke the bushwalk even months later.
evoke.basic: The smell of wet eucalyptus can bring the bushwalk back to mind.

exceed.simple: To go beyond a limit, amount, or expected level.
exceed.detailed: To be greater than a number, rule, or standard, which in science often signals a result outside the safe or predicted range.
exceed.example: If the temperature readings exceed 40 degrees, stop the lamp and record the time.
exceed.basic: If the temperature goes past 40 degrees, stop the lamp and record the time.

exhibit.simple: To show something clearly, such as a quality, result, or display.
exhibit.detailed: To present evidence of a feature or behaviour, or to put objects on view; in science it often means a sample displays a measurable property.
exhibit.example: Some metals exhibit magnetism, while others do not attract the compass needle.
exhibit.basic: Some metals show magnetism, while others do not attract the needle.

exploit.simple: To use a resource or situation, sometimes unfairly, to get an advantage.
exploit.detailed: To make use of something for gain; in HASS it can mean developing resources, but it often carries a warning about harming people or environments.
exploit.example: Miners who exploit a river catchment must still protect drinking-water quality.
exploit.basic: Miners who use a river area must still protect drinking water.

expose.simple: To uncover something so it can be seen, tested, or judged.
expose.detailed: To leave a surface, idea, or person open to light, air, danger, or public view; in science, exposing a sample changes the conditions you are testing.
expose.example: Expose one seedling to sunlight and keep the other in shade to compare growth.
expose.basic: Put one seedling in sunlight and keep the other in shade.

facilitate.simple: To make a task or process easier so it can happen more smoothly.
facilitate.detailed: To help a discussion, experiment, or plan proceed by removing obstacles or providing structure, without necessarily doing the whole job yourself.
facilitate.example: Sentence starters can facilitate discussion when a group is unsure how to begin.
facilitate.basic: Sentence starters can make discussion easier when a group does not know how to begin.

fluctuate.simple: To rise and fall, rather than staying at one steady level.
fluctuate.detailed: To change repeatedly up and down, as temperatures, prices, or populations often do when conditions are not constant.
fluctuate.example: Creek levels fluctuate after storms, so one measurement is not enough.
fluctuate.basic: Creek levels go up and down after storms, so one measurement is not enough.

foster.simple: To encourage something good to grow, such as a skill, habit, or feeling.
foster.detailed: To support development over time through care and conditions, used in HASS for community strengths and in schools for curiosity or inclusion.
foster.example: Group roles can foster cooperation if every student has a clear job.
foster.basic: Group roles can help cooperation grow if every student has a job.

hinder.simple: To make progress slower or more difficult.
hinder.detailed: To get in the way of a process, argument, or plan so the intended result is delayed or weakened.
hinder.example: Missing units on a graph can hinder a reader's ability to compare the results.
hinder.basic: Missing units on a graph can make it harder to compare the results.

illuminate.simple: To light something up, or to make an idea much clearer.
illuminate.detailed: To shed light in a literal sense, or, in literary and academic writing, to explain a meaning so readers suddenly understand it.
illuminate.example: One well-chosen quotation can illuminate the theme better than a long summary.
illuminate.basic: One well-chosen quotation can make the theme clearer than a long summary.

implement.simple: To put a plan, rule, or method into action.
implement.detailed: To carry out a decision so it actually happens in the real world, not just on paper, which is a key academic and civic verb.
implement.example: The student council will implement the new bin system after the assembly.
implement.basic: The student council will start using the new bin system after the assembly.

impose.simple: To force a rule, cost, or decision onto people, whether they want it or not.
impose.detailed: To place a requirement, tax, penalty, or view on others by authority or pressure, a frequent idea in HASS when studying governments and power.
impose.example: Councils can impose a fine if garden waste is dumped in the creek.
impose.basic: Councils can give a fine if garden waste is dumped in the creek.

incline.simple: To lean towards a particular opinion, choice, or direction.
incline.detailed: To tend to favour one option or interpretation, or to slope physically; in academic writing it usually signals a reasoned preference.
incline.example: The evidence may incline judges to support a later school start time.
incline.basic: The evidence may lead judges to support a later school start time.

incorporate.simple: To include something as a working part of a larger whole.
incorporate.detailed: To build an idea, material, or method into a system so it belongs there, from incorporating a quote into a paragraph to adding a variable into a design.
incorporate.example: Incorporate one statistic into your introduction so the problem feels real.
incorporate.basic: Put one statistic into your introduction so the problem feels real.

induce.simple: To cause a change or feeling to happen, often on purpose.
induce.detailed: To bring about a result by creating the right conditions, a precise science verb for causing a reaction, current, or behaviour.
induce.example: A moving magnet can induce a small current in the coil of wire.
induce.basic: A moving magnet can cause a small current in the coil of wire.

inhibit.simple: To slow down or stop a process from happening as strongly as it could.
inhibit.detailed: To restrain a reaction, growth, or behaviour, often used in science when a chemical, condition, or rule holds something back.
inhibit.example: Low temperature can inhibit yeast activity, so the dough rises more slowly.
inhibit.basic: Low temperature can slow yeast, so the dough rises more slowly.

initiate.simple: To start a process, plan, or action deliberately.
initiate.detailed: To set something in motion as the first official or organised step, rather than waiting for it to happen by chance.
initiate.example: Year 6 leaders will initiate a compost scheme in the first week of term.
initiate.basic: Year 6 leaders will start a compost scheme in the first week of term.

innovate.simple: To invent a new method, product, or way of doing something.
innovate.detailed: To introduce a useful change that improves on the usual approach, a science and design verb linked to creativity and problem-solving.
innovate.example: The design team had to innovate when the first water filter kept clogging.
innovate.basic: The design team had to invent a new approach when the first filter clogged.

insert.simple: To put something into a space, sentence, or system where it was not before.
insert.detailed: To place an object, word, or piece of data inside something else so it becomes part of that whole, from inserting a quote to inserting a sample.
insert.example: Insert a short quotation after your claim so the evidence sits next to the idea.
insert.basic: Put a short quotation after your claim so the evidence sits next to the idea.

institute.simple: To set up a new rule, system, or organisation so it officially begins.
institute.detailed: To establish a practice or body with authority, a formal HASS verb used when governments or schools create lasting arrangements.
institute.example: The council will institute a new water-saving programme after the drought report.
institute.basic: The council will start a new water-saving programme after the report.

interact.simple: To act on each other so that each one affects the other.
interact.detailed: To have a two-way effect, whether people talking, chemicals reacting, or living things sharing a habitat.
interact.example: In a food web, predators and prey interact, so a change in one group affects the other.
interact.basic: In a food web, predators and prey affect each other.

intervene.simple: To step in and try to change what is happening.
intervene.detailed: To become involved in a situation, often to prevent harm or to influence an outcome, a key idea in government, history, and conflict.
intervene.example: Teachers may intervene if an argument on the oval looks as if it will turn unsafe.
intervene.basic: Teachers may step in if an argument on the oval looks unsafe.

manipulate.simple: To handle or control something skilfully, or sometimes unfairly.
manipulate.detailed: To operate variables, objects, or information so they change in a planned way; in science it can be neutral, but it can also mean dishonest control.
manipulate.example: In a fair test you manipulate only one variable and keep the others constant.
manipulate.basic: In a fair test you change only one thing and keep the others the same.

mediate.simple: To help two sides talk and reach a fairer agreement.
mediate.detailed: To act as a go-between in a disagreement so each party can be heard and a workable solution can be found.
mediate.example: The year coordinator will mediate between the two teams after the unfair tackle.
mediate.basic: The year coordinator will help the two teams talk after the unfair tackle.

mitigate.simple: To make a problem less severe without removing it completely.
mitigate.detailed: To reduce harm, risk, or impact through planned actions, a precise science and civic verb used for drought, flooding, and pollution.
mitigate.example: Shade cloth can mitigate heat stress on seedlings during a heatwave.
mitigate.basic: Shade cloth can make heat less harmful for seedlings during a heatwave.

negotiate.simple: To discuss a problem until both sides can accept a plan.
negotiate.detailed: To work through competing interests with talk and compromise, used in HASS for treaties, workplace deals, and everyday civic disagreements.
negotiate.example: The two classes had to negotiate a timetable so both could use the library.
negotiate.basic: The two classes had to talk until they shared the library fairly.

notify.simple: To tell someone official or important information so they know in time.
notify.detailed: To give formal notice of a fact, change, or requirement, usually in writing or a clear announcement rather than a casual remark.
notify.example: Please notify the office if a student will miss the excursion bus.
notify.basic: Please tell the office if a student will miss the excursion bus.

offset.simple: To balance one effect with another so the overall harm or cost is smaller.
offset.detailed: To counteract a loss, emission, or disadvantage by creating an opposite benefit, a common idea in environmental science and budgeting.
offset.example: Planting trees can offset some of the carbon released by a school bus trip.
offset.basic: Planting trees can make up for some of the carbon from a bus trip.

outweigh.simple: To be more important or greater than something else when you compare them.
outweigh.detailed: To tip the balance in a judgement so one benefit, risk, or reason counts more than the opposing side.
outweigh.example: In the waste debate, long-term health benefits outweigh the short-term cost of new bins.
outweigh.basic: In the waste debate, long-term health benefits matter more than the cost of new bins.

perceive.simple: To notice or understand something through your senses or mind.
perceive.detailed: To become aware of a detail, mood, or meaning, which in literature often depends on a character's point of view as much as on the facts.
perceive.example: Readers perceive the forest as threatening because the narrator describes every shadow.
perceive.basic: Readers see the forest as threatening because the narrator describes every shadow.

persist.simple: To continue for a long time, or to keep trying despite difficulty.
persist.detailed: To remain present or active instead of stopping, used in science for weather and symptoms, and in learning for determined effort.
persist.example: If drought conditions persist, farmers may need to change what they plant.
persist.basic: If the dry weather keeps going, farmers may need to change what they plant.

portray.simple: To show a person, place, or idea in a particular way in words or images.
portray.detailed: To represent a subject so readers or viewers receive a chosen impression, which can be fair, exaggerated, or biased.
portray.example: The novel does not portray the bush as empty; it is full of sound and danger.
portray.basic: The novel does not show the bush as empty; it is full of sound and danger.

postpone.simple: To move an event to a later time instead of doing it now.
postpone.detailed: To delay a planned action on purpose, usually because conditions, information, or people are not ready.
postpone.example: The principal will postpone the sports carnival if the oval is still flooded.
postpone.basic: The principal will move the sports carnival if the oval is still flooded.

precede.simple: To happen or come before something else in time or order.
precede.detailed: To occupy an earlier position in a sequence, which helps writers explain cause, chronology, or the structure of a text.
precede.example: A clear aim should precede the method section in a scientific report.
precede.basic: A clear aim should come before the method section in a report.

prescribe.simple: To set an official rule about what must be done, or to order a treatment.
prescribe.detailed: To lay down a required action, dose, or standard with authority, used in HASS for laws and procedures as well as in medicine.
prescribe.example: Safety guidelines prescribe how many adults must travel with each bus group.
prescribe.basic: Safety guidelines say how many adults must travel with each bus group.

prevail.simple: To win out or become the most common or powerful result.
prevail.detailed: To prove stronger than opposing forces, ideas, or conditions, whether a team prevails in a contest or a custom prevails in a community.
prevail.example: In the end, the fairer argument should prevail if the judges weigh the evidence.
prevail.basic: In the end, the fairer argument should win if the judges weigh the evidence.

prohibit.simple: To officially forbid an action so it is not allowed.
prohibit.detailed: To ban something by law, rule, or authority, a precise civic verb that is stronger than simply discouraging a behaviour.
prohibit.example: National park rules prohibit visitors from feeding the wildlife.
prohibit.basic: National park rules do not allow visitors to feed the wildlife.

prompt.simple: To cause someone to act or speak, often quickly or as a reminder.
prompt.detailed: To trigger a response, question, or action; in class a sentence starter can do this, while in argument a news story can spark a protest.
prompt.example: The surprising graph will prompt students to ask what changed in the second week.
prompt.basic: The surprising graph will make students ask what changed in the second week.

provoke.simple: To stir a strong feeling or reaction, sometimes on purpose.
provoke.detailed: To cause anger, thought, or action by words or events; in literature a sharp remark can start a conflict that reveals character.
provoke.example: A careless joke can provoke an argument that the writer then has to resolve.
provoke.basic: A careless joke can start an argument that the writer then has to resolve.

qualify.simple: To meet the standard needed for a role, team, or prize.
qualify.detailed: To become eligible by reaching a required level, or, in careful argument, to limit a statement so it is not too absolute.
qualify.example: Two more accurate times will help her qualify for the district athletics final.
qualify.basic: Two more accurate times will help her reach the district athletics final.

quantify.simple: To describe something with numbers so you can measure or compare it.
quantify.detailed: To express an amount, change, or effect numerically rather than with vague words such as 'a lot' or 'some'.
quantify.example: The report must quantify the drop in waste, not just say the bins looked emptier.
quantify.basic: The report must give a number for the drop in waste.

reconcile.simple: To restore peace after a disagreement, or to make two facts fit together.
reconcile.detailed: To settle a conflict or resolve an apparent contradiction so relationships, records, or explanations become consistent again.
reconcile.example: The two captains tried to reconcile after the disputed try so the season could continue.
reconcile.basic: The two captains tried to make peace after the disputed try.

reconstruct.simple: To build something again, or to piece the past together from clues.
reconstruct.detailed: To restore a structure, event, or argument from remaining evidence, a key skill in history when original records are incomplete.
reconstruct.example: Historians reconstruct daily life in the colony from letters, tools, and maps.
reconstruct.basic: Historians piece daily life in the colony together from letters, tools, and maps.

reconsider.simple: To think about a decision again, in case it should change.
reconsider.detailed: To review a judgement with fresh attention or new evidence rather than clinging to the first idea.
reconsider.example: New rainfall data may make the council reconsider the dam-building plan.
reconsider.basic: New rainfall data may make the council think again about the dam plan.

regulate.simple: To control an activity with rules so it stays safe, fair, or orderly.
regulate.detailed: To manage a system through standards and oversight, from governments regulating industry to the body regulating temperature.
regulate.example: The government can regulate fishing so species are not taken faster than they breed.
regulate.basic: The government can set fishing rules so species are not taken too fast.

reiterate.simple: To say the same important point again so it is not missed.
reiterate.detailed: To repeat a claim or instruction for emphasis, useful in argument when a writer wants the audience to remember a key reason.
reiterate.example: Let me reiterate that every claim in the debate needs a source.
reiterate.basic: Let me say again that every claim in the debate needs a source.

relinquish.simple: To give up a right, role, or object, usually on purpose.
relinquish.detailed: To surrender control or possession, often after a decision or under pressure, a formal HASS verb used for power, land, or claims.
relinquish.example: A leader may relinquish a position if the community no longer supports the plan.
relinquish.basic: A leader may give up a position if the community no longer supports the plan.

render.simple: To make someone or something become a certain way, or to present it vividly.
render.detailed: In literary writing, to cause a state or to depict a scene so readers experience it; the verb can also mean to give a service or judgement.
render.example: The final image of empty streets can render the victory strangely sad.
render.basic: The final image of empty streets can make the victory feel strangely sad.

replicate.simple: To copy a result or method so you can check that it happens again.
replicate.detailed: To repeat an experiment or process under similar conditions, which is how scientists test whether a finding is reliable.
replicate.example: Another group should replicate the test before we trust the unusual result.
replicate.basic: Another group should do the test again before we trust the unusual result.

resemble.simple: To look or seem like something else in an important way.
resemble.detailed: To share noticeable features with another object, organism, or idea, which helps scientists classify and writers build comparisons.
resemble.example: The fossil teeth resemble those of a modern shark, so the diet may have been similar.
resemble.basic: The fossil teeth look like those of a modern shark.

resume.simple: To start again after a pause or interruption.
resume.detailed: To continue an activity from the point where it stopped, a precise academic verb for lessons, talks, and processes.
resume.example: We will resume the investigation after lunch when the ice has been prepared.
resume.basic: We will start the investigation again after lunch.

retrieve.simple: To get something back after it was stored, lost, or left behind.
retrieve.detailed: To recover an object, memory, or piece of information so it can be used again, from retrieving a file to retrieving a sample.
retrieve.example: Students must retrieve their draft from the shared folder before the editing lesson.
retrieve.basic: Students must get their draft back from the shared folder before editing.

sacrifice.simple: To give up something valuable so that a more important goal can succeed.
sacrifice.detailed: To accept a loss of time, comfort, or possession for a person, cause, or greater good, a strong literary and moral idea.
sacrifice.example: The older sister chose to sacrifice her spare ticket so her brother could go.
sacrifice.basic: The older sister gave up her spare ticket so her brother could go.

scrutinise.simple: To examine something very closely to find strengths, errors, or hidden details.
scrutinise.detailed: To inspect evidence, a text, or a plan with critical attention, a high-value academic verb for scholarship reading and scientific checking.
scrutinise.example: Markers will scrutinise your conclusion to see whether it actually matches the table.
scrutinise.basic: Markers will look very closely at your conclusion to see if it matches the table.

simulate.simple: To copy a real process in a safer or simpler model so you can study it.
simulate.detailed: To imitate conditions or behaviour, often with a diagram, role-play, or computer model, when the real event is too large, slow, or dangerous.
simulate.example: The class used ice and a lamp to simulate how sunlight melts Antarctic ice.
simulate.basic: The class used ice and a lamp to copy how sunlight melts Antarctic ice.

stimulate.simple: To wake up or increase activity in a person, idea, or living system.
stimulate.detailed: To encourage a response so something works more strongly, from stimulating discussion to stimulating nerve cells or plant growth.
stimulate.example: A surprising question can stimulate discussion more effectively than a yes-or-no prompt.
stimulate.basic: A surprising question can get discussion started better than a yes-or-no prompt.

submit.simple: To hand in work for marking, or to give in to a stronger force.
submit.detailed: To present a document or proposal officially, or to yield after pressure; in school the first sense is the usual academic meaning.
submit.example: Please submit the science report by Friday so feedback can arrive before the test.
submit.basic: Please hand in the science report by Friday so feedback can arrive before the test.

substitute.simple: To use one thing in place of another when the first is missing or weaker.
substitute.detailed: To replace a material, word, or person with an alternative that can do a similar job, a useful science and writing verb.
substitute.example: You can substitute honey for sugar, but the browning time may change.
substitute.basic: You can use honey instead of sugar, but the browning time may change.

supplement.simple: To add something extra so the original is stronger or more complete.
supplement.detailed: To provide an additional part that fills a gap, from extra evidence in an essay to extra nutrients in a diet.
supplement.example: Photographs can supplement the written observations in a field journal.
supplement.basic: Photographs can add extra detail to the written observations.

suppress.simple: To hold something down so it does not spread, appear, or get heard.
suppress.detailed: To prevent a feeling, report, protest, or process from becoming public or powerful, a strong HASS verb about control and power.
suppress.example: A government that tries to suppress news of a disaster often loses public trust.
suppress.basic: A government that tries to hide news of a disaster often loses public trust.

surpass.simple: To do better than a person, record, or expected level.
surpass.detailed: To go beyond a previous standard of quality or quantity, used for results, performances, and achievements.
surpass.example: This year's recycling total may surpass last year's if every class uses the correct bin.
surpass.basic: This year's recycling total may beat last year's if every class uses the correct bin.

suspend.simple: To stop something for a time, with the idea that it may start again later.
suspend.detailed: To pause an activity, rule, or person's participation temporarily, a formal civic and school verb different from ending something forever.
suspend.example: The council will suspend outdoor sport if the air quality becomes unsafe.
suspend.basic: The council will stop outdoor sport for a while if the air becomes unsafe.

terminate.simple: To bring something to a complete end, rather than pausing it.
terminate.detailed: To finish a process, contract, or activity so it does not continue, a formal academic verb stronger than simply stopping for a break.
terminate.example: The teacher will terminate the trial if any chemical spills outside the tray.
terminate.basic: The teacher will end the trial if any chemical spills outside the tray.

testify.simple: To give a formal statement about what you know or saw, especially as a witness.
testify.detailed: To speak as evidence before a court, inquiry, or official hearing, a key HASS verb about law, truth, and responsibility.
testify.example: A neighbour may testify about the flood height if the council holds an inquiry.
testify.basic: A neighbour may tell the inquiry how high the flood water rose.

transcend.simple: To go beyond ordinary limits and reach something greater.
transcend.detailed: To rise above a boundary of time, culture, or difficulty, a literary verb used when an idea or feeling seems larger than the moment.
transcend.example: The friendship in the novel seems to transcend the feud that divided the two families.
transcend.basic: The friendship in the novel seems bigger than the feud that divided the families.

transmit.simple: To send something from one place, person, or system to another.
transmit.detailed: To pass on energy, information, disease, or a signal so it travels between points, a precise science and communication verb.
transmit.example: Copper wires transmit electricity more efficiently than many other metals.
transmit.basic: Copper wires send electricity more efficiently than many other metals.

undermine.simple: To weaken something gradually, often from underneath or in a hidden way.
undermine.detailed: To damage the strength, trust, or success of a plan, argument, or person, sometimes without an open attack.
undermine.example: A missing source can undermine an otherwise careful persuasive essay.
undermine.basic: A missing source can weaken an otherwise careful persuasive essay.

unify.simple: To bring separate parts or people together into one group or system.
unify.detailed: To create unity from difference, used in HASS for nations, movements, and communities that join under shared rules or goals.
unify.example: Federation was meant to unify the colonies under one national parliament.
unify.basic: Federation was meant to bring the colonies together under one parliament.

utilise.simple: To make practical use of something for a clear purpose.
utilise.detailed: To put a resource, skill, or method to work, a formal academic verb that should replace 'use' only when the purpose is precise.
utilise.example: The design brief asks students to utilise recycled materials in the model bridge.
utilise.basic: The design brief asks students to use recycled materials in the model bridge.

withstand.simple: To stay strong against force, pressure, or difficult conditions.
withstand.detailed: To resist damage or collapse when something pushes, heats, or tests you, used for materials, buildings, and living things.
withstand.example: A seawall must withstand storm waves if the coastal road is to stay open.
withstand.basic: A seawall must stay strong against storm waves if the coastal road is to stay open.

yield.simple: To produce a result, crop, or amount, or to give way under pressure.
yield.detailed: In science, to give an output such as data, energy, or harvest; the same verb can also mean to surrender, so context matters.
yield.example: The second trial should yield a clearer result if we keep the starting temperature the same.
yield.basic: The second trial should give a clearer result if we keep the starting temperature the same.

abstract.simple: A short summary at the start of a report that tells the main aim and findings.
abstract.detailed: A concise overview of a longer text, used so a reader can decide quickly what the study investigated and what it concluded.
abstract.example: Read the abstract first so you know the aim before you study the full method.
abstract.basic: Read the short summary first so you know the aim before the full method.

adaptation.simple: A feature or change that helps a living thing survive in its environment.
adaptation.detailed: A trait, behaviour, or adjustment that improves survival or success in particular conditions; the word can also mean a story changed for a new form.
adaptation.example: A camel's ability to store fat in its hump is an adaptation to desert life.
adaptation.basic: A camel's hump is a feature that helps it live in the desert.

agency.simple: An organisation that does a particular public job, or a person's power to act.
agency.detailed: In HASS it often names an official body that carries out work, and it can also mean the capacity of people to make choices that shape events.
agency.example: The weather agency issued a heatwave warning two days before the carnival.
agency.basic: The weather office issued a heatwave warning two days before the carnival.

allegiance.simple: Loyalty and support given to a person, group, country, or idea.
allegiance.detailed: A committed bond of duty or faithfulness, discussed in HASS when people choose sides in politics, history, or community life.
allegiance.example: Soldiers in the colony were expected to show allegiance to the Crown.
allegiance.basic: Soldiers in the colony were expected to stay loyal to the Crown.

alliance.simple: An agreement between groups or countries to work together for a shared aim.
alliance.detailed: A formal or informal partnership formed so members can support one another, often in politics, war, trade, or community campaigns.
alliance.example: The two coastal towns formed an alliance to share the cost of a new seawall.
alliance.basic: The two coastal towns agreed to work together to pay for a new seawall.

allusion.simple: A brief mention of a well-known story, person, or event without explaining it fully.
allusion.detailed: An indirect reference that expects the reader to recognise the original, adding meaning in literature if the audience shares that knowledge.
allusion.example: Calling the oval 'our Gallipoli' was an allusion that made the match sound like a hard battle.
allusion.basic: Calling the oval 'our Gallipoli' hinted at a famous hard battle.

analogy.simple: A comparison that explains a new idea by linking it to something familiar.
analogy.detailed: A reasoned likeness between two things, used in teaching and argument to make an unfamiliar process easier to understand.
analogy.example: The teacher used an analogy between a battery and a water tank to explain stored energy.
analogy.basic: The teacher compared a battery to a water tank to explain stored energy.

anomaly.simple: A result or fact that does not fit the usual pattern and needs checking.
anomaly.detailed: A departure from what is expected, which in science may signal an error, a new variable, or a genuine discovery.
anomaly.example: One very high reading was an anomaly, so the group repeated that trial.
anomaly.basic: One very high reading did not fit, so the group repeated that trial.

anthology.simple: A book that collects chosen poems, stories, or extracts by one or more writers.
anthology.detailed: A curated volume of literary pieces, useful in English when students compare different voices on a shared theme.
anthology.example: Our class anthology includes bush poems beside modern city stories.
anthology.basic: Our class collection includes bush poems beside modern city stories.

appendix.simple: An extra section at the end of a book or report that holds useful extra detail.
appendix.detailed: Supporting material placed after the main text, such as raw data, maps, or full questionnaires, so the argument stays clear.
appendix.example: Put the full survey questions in the appendix so the report itself stays short.
appendix.basic: Put the full survey questions at the end so the report itself stays short.

architecture.simple: The design of buildings, or the way the parts of a system are arranged.
architecture.detailed: The art and planning of structures, and by extension the organised design of institutions, cities, or ideas in HASS texts.
architecture.example: Federation-era architecture in the main street still shows the town's early wealth.
architecture.basic: The old buildings in the main street still show the town's early wealth.

archive.simple: A collection of historical records stored so people can study them later.
archive.detailed: An organised store of documents, images, or data kept for evidence and research, often by libraries, councils, or museums.
archive.example: The town archive still holds the original letters about the 1890s drought.
archive.basic: The town still keeps the original letters about the 1890s drought.

article.simple: A piece of writing in a newspaper, magazine, or journal about one topic.
article.detailed: A structured non-fiction text that reports, explains, or argues, a common academic reading type in scholarship papers.
article.example: The newspaper article on river health used interviews as well as water-test results.
article.basic: The newspaper piece on river health used interviews as well as water-test results.

aspiration.simple: A strong hope to achieve something worthwhile in the future.
aspiration.detailed: An ambitious aim that guides effort over time, often revealing a character's values in literary and biographical writing.
aspiration.example: Her main aspiration was to become the first doctor in her family.
aspiration.basic: Her main hope was to become the first doctor in her family.

assertion.simple: A statement that something is true, made firmly but not yet proved.
assertion.detailed: A claim put forward with confidence; in argument it must be supported with evidence or it remains only an opinion.
assertion.example: An assertion about homework is weaker than a claim backed by two studies.
assertion.basic: A firm statement about homework is weaker than a claim backed by two studies.

asset.simple: Something valuable that a person, group, or country owns or can use.
asset.detailed: A useful resource, skill, or possession that provides benefit, from money and land to a team's honesty or a wetland's wildlife.
asset.example: The wetland is a community asset because it filters water and shelters birds.
asset.basic: The wetland is valuable to the community because it filters water and shelters birds.

attitude.simple: The way a person usually thinks or feels about something, shown in words and actions.
attitude.detailed: A settled outlook that shapes behaviour, tone, and choices; in literature it helps readers judge a character's values.
attitude.example: The narrator's attitude towards the new town shifts from suspicion to belonging.
attitude.basic: The narrator's feelings about the new town shift from suspicion to belonging.

audit.simple: A careful official check of records, money, or how well a system is working.
audit.detailed: A systematic review that tests whether accounts, processes, or claims match the evidence, used in government, schools, and business.
audit.example: The energy audit showed that lights left on overnight wasted the most power.
audit.basic: The careful check showed that lights left on overnight wasted the most power.

autonomy.simple: The freedom to make your own decisions without being controlled by others.
autonomy.detailed: The right or capacity of a person, group, or region to govern itself, a central idea in HASS discussions of rights and government.
autonomy.example: The new student council wants more autonomy over how fundraising money is spent.
autonomy.basic: The new student council wants more freedom over how fundraising money is spent.

benchmark.simple: A clear standard used to judge how good a result or performance is.
benchmark.detailed: A reference point for comparison, so progress can be measured against an agreed level rather than a vague feeling.
benchmark.example: Last year's recycling total became the benchmark for this term's waste target.
benchmark.basic: Last year's recycling total became the standard for this term's waste target.

biodiversity.simple: The variety of living things in a place, from tiny insects to large plants and animals.
biodiversity.detailed: The range of species, genes, and ecosystems in an area; a rich mix of living things usually makes a habitat more resilient to change.
biodiversity.example: Clearing the creek bank reduced biodiversity because fewer insects and birds remained.
biodiversity.basic: Clearing the creek bank left fewer kinds of insects and birds.

biography.simple: A true account of a real person's life, written by someone else.
biography.detailed: A non-fiction narrative that selects key events, influences, and achievements to explain how a life unfolded and why it matters.
biography.example: The biography of Eddie Mabo explains why his legal fight changed land rights.
biography.basic: The life story of Eddie Mabo explains why his legal fight changed land rights.

bureaucracy.simple: A system of officials and rules that manages government or a large organisation.
bureaucracy.detailed: The administrative structure that applies procedures, paperwork, and hierarchy; it can keep work orderly or make it slow.
bureaucracy.example: A slow bureaucracy delayed the flood-relief payments for several weeks.
bureaucracy.basic: Slow official paperwork delayed the flood-relief payments for several weeks.

capability.simple: The skill or power to do a particular kind of work well.
capability.detailed: A developed capacity, whether of a person, team, or system, to achieve a task under given conditions.
capability.example: The design task tested each group's capability to build a bridge that held one kilogram.
capability.basic: The design task tested whether each group could build a bridge that held one kilogram.

catalyst.simple: Something that speeds up a change without being used up, or that starts a bigger event.
catalyst.detailed: In science, a substance that increases the rate of a reaction; in wider writing, a person or event that triggers rapid change.
catalyst.example: The enzyme acted as a catalyst and the reaction finished in half the time.
catalyst.basic: The enzyme sped up the reaction so it finished in half the time.

census.simple: An official count of all the people living in a country or area, plus key facts about them.
census.detailed: A nationwide survey used by governments to plan services, representation, and resources from the collected population data.
census.example: Census data help councils decide how many new classrooms a suburb may need.
census.basic: The official population count helps councils decide how many new classrooms a suburb may need.

chronicle.simple: A record of events written in the order they happened.
chronicle.detailed: A historical account organised by time rather than by argument, useful for seeing sequence even when causes are still debated.
chronicle.example: The ship's chronicle listed every port from London to Sydney in date order.
chronicle.basic: The ship's record listed every port from London to Sydney in date order.

civilisation.simple: A large, organised society with cities, shared rules, and lasting culture.
civilisation.detailed: A complex community marked by government, writing or records, specialised work, and cultural achievements that can be studied across time.
civilisation.example: River valleys helped an early civilisation grow because the soil could feed many people.
civilisation.basic: River valleys helped an early organised society grow because the soil could feed many people.

classification.simple: The act of sorting things into groups that share important features.
classification.detailed: A system for naming and organising items so scientists, librarians, or writers can compare them accurately.
classification.example: The classification of leaves by vein pattern helped the class identify each tree.
classification.basic: Sorting the leaves by vein pattern helped the class identify each tree.

coalition.simple: A temporary partnership of groups that join to achieve a shared political or civic goal.
coalition.detailed: An alliance formed so separate parties or organisations can pool power, often to pass a law, win an election, or run a campaign.
coalition.example: A coalition of parents and shop owners asked the council for a safer crossing.
coalition.basic: A group of parents and shop owners asked the council for a safer crossing.

code.simple: A set of rules that tells people how they are expected to behave.
code.detailed: An organised collection of laws, standards, or principles, such as a conduct rulebook or a set of legal rules, used to guide civic life.
code.example: The school's code of conduct requires students to report bullying to a teacher.
code.basic: The school's behaviour rules require students to report bullying to a teacher.

collaboration.simple: Working with others on a shared task so the result is better than working alone.
collaboration.detailed: A planned partnership in which people combine skills, ideas, and effort, valued in academic group work and civic projects.
collaboration.example: The science prize rewarded collaboration because no single student could collect all the data.
collaboration.basic: The science prize rewarded teamwork because no single student could collect all the data.

colleague.simple: A person you work with, especially in a professional or school setting.
colleague.detailed: A fellow worker who shares duties or a workplace, a precise academic word for adults and older students in formal writing.
colleague.example: The ranger asked a colleague to check the trap while she recorded the bird calls.
colleague.basic: The ranger asked a workmate to check the trap while she recorded the bird calls.

colonist.simple: A person who settles in a new land that is controlled by another country.
colonist.detailed: Someone who lives in a colony, often taking land and resources already used by First Nations peoples, a key HASS figure in Australian history.
colonist.example: A British colonist in 1788 arrived in a land already cared for by Aboriginal nations.
colonist.basic: A British settler in 1788 arrived in a land already cared for by Aboriginal nations.

commentary.simple: Spoken or written remarks that explain, judge, or describe what is happening.
commentary.detailed: An interpretive layer added to events or a text, from sports description to a literary essay that comments on a writer's choices.
commentary.example: Your literary commentary should explain why the author repeats the word 'dust'.
commentary.basic: Your written remarks should explain why the author repeats the word 'dust'.

commission.simple: An official group given a special job, or a formal request to create something.
commission.detailed: A body appointed to investigate or manage an issue, and also the act of ordering work such as a report, artwork, or inquiry.
commission.example: A royal commission can examine a national problem that ordinary courts have not settled.
commission.basic: A special official group can examine a national problem that ordinary courts have not settled.

commitment.simple: A promise to stay with a person, task, or idea and give it real effort.
commitment.detailed: A durable obligation or dedication, whether legal, personal, or civic, that shows someone will not drop a responsibility lightly.
commitment.example: Cleaning the creek each term shows a real commitment to the local environment.
commitment.basic: Cleaning the creek each term shows a real promise to look after the local environment.

commodity.simple: A useful product that is bought, sold, or traded, such as wheat, wool, or oil.
commodity.detailed: A good that has market value and can be exchanged, a key HASS term when studying trade, farming, and resources.
commodity.example: Wheat is an important Australian commodity because so much of it is exported.
commodity.basic: Wheat is an important Australian product because so much of it is exported.

commonwealth.simple: A political community formed for the common good, and the official name of Australia as a nation.
commonwealth.detailed: A union of states or peoples organised for shared government; Australians use it for the national level of government after Federation.
commonwealth.example: After 1901 the Commonwealth government could make laws for the whole nation.
commonwealth.basic: After 1901 the national government could make laws for the whole country.

communication.simple: The sharing of information, ideas, or feelings between people or systems.
communication.detailed: The process of sending and receiving meaning through speech, writing, images, or signals, essential in academic group work and civic life.
communication.example: Clear communication between group members stopped the experiment from being repeated twice.
communication.basic: Clear talking and notes between group members stopped the experiment from being repeated twice.

compensation.simple: Something given to make up for a loss, injury, or extra effort.
compensation.detailed: Payment or another benefit provided to restore fairness after harm, work, or sacrifice, a common HASS idea in law and employment.
compensation.example: Farmers sought compensation after the flood destroyed the winter crop.
compensation.basic: Farmers asked to be paid back after the flood destroyed the winter crop.

competence.simple: The ability to do a task to a required standard.
competence.detailed: A reliable level of skill and understanding that lets someone perform work correctly and independently.
competence.example: The swimming test checks competence in deep water before the beach excursion.
competence.basic: The swimming test checks that students can manage in deep water before the beach excursion.

compliance.simple: The act of following a rule, request, or law.
compliance.detailed: Behaviour that matches required standards, often checked by officials; it can be willing or forced.
compliance.example: The building inspection checked compliance with the fire-exit rules.
compliance.basic: The building inspection checked that the fire-exit rules were being followed.

composition.simple: A piece of writing or music, or the way the parts of something are put together.
composition.detailed: In literary study it usually means a crafted text; it can also name the makeup of a mixture, group, or image.
composition.example: Her composition used short sentences to make the storm feel sudden.
composition.basic: Her piece of writing used short sentences to make the storm feel sudden.

compromise.simple: An agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wanted.
compromise.detailed: A negotiated middle position that settles a conflict without a total win, a practical civic skill in families, councils, and parliaments.
compromise.example: A compromise let one class use the hall on Monday and the other on Wednesday.
compromise.basic: A middle-ground deal let one class use the hall on Monday and the other on Wednesday.

computation.simple: The process of working out an answer using numbers or a clear method.
computation.detailed: A calculated procedure that turns data into a result, whether done by hand, on paper, or with a machine.
computation.example: Show every step of the computation so the marker can see how the mean was found.
computation.basic: Show every step of the working so the marker can see how the mean was found.

concession.simple: Something you admit or give up, often to be fair or to help a deal succeed.
concession.detailed: In argument, an acknowledgement of a weaker point or an opposing truth; in civic life, a right or benefit granted after negotiation.
concession.example: A fair essay includes a concession before explaining why the main claim is still stronger.
concession.basic: A fair essay admits one weaker point before explaining why the main claim is still stronger.

confidence.simple: A calm belief that you can do something, or that someone or something can be trusted.
confidence.detailed: Trust in a person, process, or one's own ability; in literature it can rise or collapse and change a character's choices.
confidence.example: The shy narrator gains confidence after the first successful speech.
confidence.basic: The shy narrator feels braver after the first successful speech.

consensus.simple: General agreement reached by a group after discussion.
consensus.detailed: A shared decision or view that most members can accept, even if it is not everyone's first choice.
consensus.example: After three meetings the class reached a consensus to ban balloons at the fete.
consensus.basic: After three meetings the class agreed together to ban balloons at the fete.

consistency.simple: The quality of staying the same in quality, method, or message over time.
consistency.detailed: Reliability and internal agreement, so results, rules, or arguments do not jump about without reason.
consistency.example: Consistency in measuring the plants at the same time each day made the graph fairer.
consistency.basic: Measuring the plants at the same time each day made the graph fairer.

constituency.simple: The group of voters, or the area, that an elected representative serves.
constituency.detailed: An electoral district and the people who live there, a core HASS term for understanding democracy and representation.
constituency.example: Each member of parliament must listen to the needs of their own constituency.
constituency.basic: Each member of parliament must listen to the needs of their own voting area.

constraint.simple: A limit that stops you from doing whatever you like.
constraint.detailed: A restriction of time, money, space, or rules that shapes what is possible in a design, argument, or investigation.
constraint.example: A time constraint of twenty minutes forced the group to choose one test only.
constraint.basic: Having only twenty minutes forced the group to choose one test only.

construction.simple: The process of building something, or the way a text or idea is put together.
construction.detailed: Physical building work, and also the crafted structure of an argument, identity, or historical account in HASS and English.
construction.example: Road construction near the school changed the walking route for a whole term.
construction.basic: Road building near the school changed the walking route for a whole term.

consultant.simple: A person paid for specialist advice because they know a field well.
consultant.detailed: An expert who is invited to examine a problem and recommend action, common in government, schools, and business projects.
consultant.example: The school hired a traffic consultant to design a safer kiss-and-drop zone.
consultant.basic: The school hired an expert to design a safer kiss-and-drop zone.
